claim: KNOX and BELL transcription factors regulate distinct steps of diploid development in plants.
source: KNOX and BELL transcription factors regulate distinct steps of diploid development in plants.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract summarizing established knowledge about KNOX and BELL functions.

claim: In Chlamydomonas reinhardtii, KNOX and BELL proteins are inherited by gametes of the opposite mating types.
source: In the green alga Chlamydomonas reinhardtii, KNOX and BELL proteins are inherited by gametes of the opposite mating types and heterodimerize in zygotes to activate diploid development.
evidence: This statement references established findings about C. reinhardtii from prior literature.

claim: In Chlamydomonas reinhardtii, KNOX and BELL proteins heterodimerize in zygotes to activate diploid development.
source: In the green alga Chlamydomonas reinhardtii, KNOX and BELL proteins are inherited by gametes of the opposite mating types and heterodimerize in zygotes to activate diploid development.
evidence: This statement references established findings about C. reinhardtii from prior literature.

claim: In Physcomitrium patens, KNOX and BELL proteins function in sporophyte and spore formation.
source: By contrast, in land plants such as Physcomitrium patens and Arabidopsis thaliana, KNOX and BELL proteins function in sporophyte and spore formation, meristem maintenance and organogenesis during the later stages of diploid development.
evidence: This statement references established findings about P. patens from prior literature.

claim: In Arabidopsis thaliana, KNOX and BELL proteins function in meristem maintenance and organogenesis during the later stages of diploid development.
source: By contrast, in land plants such as Physcomitrium patens and Arabidopsis thaliana, KNOX and BELL proteins function in sporophyte and spore formation, meristem maintenance and organogenesis during the later stages of diploid development.
evidence: This statement references established findings about Arabidopsis from prior literature.

claim: In Marchantia polymorpha, gamete-expressed KNOX and BELL are required to initiate zygotic development by promoting nuclear fusion.
source: Here, we show that in the basal land plant species Marchantia polymorpha, gamete-expressed KNOX and BELL are required to initiate zygotic development by promoting nuclear fusion in a manner strikingly similar to that in C. reinhardtii.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by genetic and imaging data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The mechanism of zygote activation by KNOX and BELL in Marchantia polymorpha is strikingly similar to that in Chlamydomonas reinhardtii.
source: Here, we show that in the basal land plant species Marchantia polymorpha, gamete-expressed KNOX and BELL are required to initiate zygotic development by promoting nuclear fusion in a manner strikingly similar to that in C. reinhardtii.
evidence: This is a comparative conclusion drawn from the experimental data and literature.

claim: Zygote activation is the ancestral role of KNOX/BELL transcription factors.
source: Our results indicate that zygote activation is the ancestral role of KNOX/BELL transcription factors, which shifted toward meristem maintenance as land plants evolved.
evidence: This is an evolutionary inference based on the comparative data from M. polymorpha and C. reinhardtii.

claim: The role of KNOX/BELL transcription factors shifted toward meristem maintenance as land plants evolved.
source: Our results indicate that zygote activation is the ancestral role of KNOX/BELL transcription factors, which shifted toward meristem maintenance as land plants evolved.
evidence: This is an evolutionary inference based on the comparative data across plant lineages.

claim: In land plants, both the haploid and diploid phases are multicellular, producing gametophytic and sporophytic bodies, respectively.
source: In land plants, both the haploid and diploid phases are multicellular, producing gametophytic and sporophytic bodies, respectively.
evidence: This is established knowledge about land plant life cycles.

claim: In bryophytes including liverworts, mosses, and hornworts, gametophytes are larger and more morphologically complex than sporophytes.
source: In bryophytes including liverworts, mosses, and hornworts, gametophytes are larger and more morphologically complex than sporophytes, which consist of only a few cell types.
evidence: This is established knowledge about bryophyte morphology.

claim: Bryophyte sporophytes consist of only a few cell types.
source: In bryophytes including liverworts, mosses, and hornworts, gametophytes are larger and more morphologically complex than sporophytes, which consist of only a few cell types.
evidence: This is established knowledge about bryophyte sporophyte structure.

claim: During land plant evolution, the life cycle shifted toward a sporophyte-dominant style to facilitate adaptation to terrestrial environments.
source: During the course of land plant evolution, the life cycle shifted toward a sporophyte-dominant style, presumably to facilitate adaptation to terrestrial environments where it is advantageous to generate large sporophytes that produce many spores.
evidence: This is an evolutionary hypothesis based on established knowledge and inference.

claim: The sporophytes of extant flowering plants exhibit far more complex morphologies than their male and female gametophytes.
source: Consequently, the sporophytes of extant flowering plants (angiosperms) exhibit far more complex morphologies than their male and female gametophytes, the pollen grain, and embryo sac, respectively, which are composed of only a few cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about angiosperm morphology.

claim: Angiosperm gametophytes (pollen grain and embryo sac) are composed of only a few cells.
source: Consequently, the sporophytes of extant flowering plants (angiosperms) exhibit far more complex morphologies than their male and female gametophytes, the pollen grain, and embryo sac, respectively, which are composed of only a few cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about angiosperm gametophyte structure.

claim: The evolutionary transition in life cycle was facilitated by the cooption of genes and/or gene regulatory networks that regulate gametophyte development to function in sporophyte development.
source: This evolutionary transition in life cycle is thought to have been facilitated by the cooption of genes and/or gene regulatory networks that regulate gametophyte development to function in sporophyte development (Bowman et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from the literature cited.

claim: Key steps of life cycle progression have continued to be driven by conserved regulators during land plant evolution.
source: However, key steps of life cycle progression per se have continued to be driven by conserved regulators during land plant evolution, as recently reported for gametophytic sexual differentiation and gamete formation (Koi et al., 2016; Rövekamp et al., 2016, Higo et al., 2018; Yamaoka et al., 2018; Hisanaga et al., 2019a; Hisanaga et al., 2019b).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to recent literature.

claim: Homeodomain transcription factors are developmental regulators that are evolutionarily conserved in eukaryotes.
source: Homeodomain transcription factors (HD TFs) are developmental regulators that are evolutionarily conserved in eukaryotes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about HD TFs.

claim: HD TFs are classified into two families, TALE and non-TALE, based on amino acid sequence similarity in the HD domain.
source: HD TFs are classified into two families, three-amino-acid-loop-extension (TALE) and non-TALE, based on amino acid sequence similarity in the HD domain (Bertolino et al., 1995; Derelle et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited literature.

claim: In Saccharomyces cerevisiae and Coprinopsis cinerea, TALE and non-TALE HD TFs are expressed in haploid cells of opposite mating types.
source: In the fungi Saccharomyces cerevisiae and Coprinopsis cinerea, TALE and non-TALE HD TFs are expressed in haploid cells of opposite mating types (Herskowitz, 1989; Kues et al., 1992).
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited literature.

claim: In fungi, TALE and non-TALE HD TFs heterodimerize in zygotes to regulate the expression of genes promoting the haploid-to-diploid transition.
source: These proteins heterodimerize in zygotes to regulate the expression of genes promoting the haloid-to-diploid transition (Goutte and Johnson, 1988; Spit et al., 1998).
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited literature.

claim: In green plants, TALE HD TFs have diversified into the KNOX and BELL subfamilies.
source: In green plants, TALE HD TFs have diversified into the KNOX (KNOTTED1-LIKE HOMEOBOX) and BELL (BELL-LIKE) subfamilies.
evidence: This is established knowledge about plant HD TF evolution.

claim: In Chlamydomonas reinhardtii, the KNOX protein GSM1 accumulates in the cytosol of minus gametes.
source: In the unicellular green alga Chlamydomonas reinhardtii, the KNOX protein GAMETE SPECIFIC MINUS1 (GSM1) and the BELL protein GAMETE SPECIFIC PLUS1 (GSP1) accumulate in the cytosol of minus and plus gametes, respectively.
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior literature on C. reinhardtii.

claim: In Chlamydomonas reinhardtii, the BELL protein GSP1 accumulates in the cytosol of plus gametes.
source: In the unicellular green alga Chlamydomonas reinhardtii, the KNOX protein GAMETE SPECIFIC MINUS1 (GSM1) and the BELL protein GAMETE SPECIFIC PLUS1 (GSP1) accumulate in the cytosol of minus and plus gametes, respectively.
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior literature on C. reinhardtii.

claim: Upon fertilization in Chlamydomonas reinhardtii, GSM1 and GSP1 heterodimerize and translocate to both male and female pronuclei to activate the expression of early zygote-specific genes.
source: Upon fertilization, the two proteins heterodimerize and translocate to both male and female pronuclei to activate the expression of early zygote-specific genes.
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior literature on C. reinhardtii.

claim: Loss-of-function mutations in GSP1 or GSM1 in Chlamydomonas reinhardtii result in pleiotropic phenotypes involving cellular rearrangements in zygotes.
source: Loss-of-function mutations in either GSP1 or GSM1 result in pleiotropic phenotypes involving cellular rearrangements in zygotes, such as the loss of nuclear and mitochondrial fusion, lack of selective degradation of minus-derived chloroplast DNA and chloroplast membrane fusion, and defects in flagellar resorption (Joo et al., 2017; Kariyawasam et al., 2019; Lee et al., 2008; Lopez et al., 2015; Nishimura et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge from multiple cited studies.

claim: In land plants, KNOX proteins are diversified into class I (KNOX1) and class II (KNOX2).
source: In land plants, KNOX proteins are further diversified into class I (KNOX1) and class II (KNOX2) (Kerstetter et al., 1994; Mukherjee et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited literature.

claim: KNOX1 proteins promote cell proliferation in the meristematic tissues of aerial organs in angiosperms.
source: Based on their expression patterns and the phenotypes of both knockout and overexpression lines, KNOX1 proteins are thought to promote cell proliferation in the meristematic tissues of aerial organs.
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior studies in angiosperms.

claim: KNOX2 genes act antagonistically to KNOX1 to promote cell differentiation.
source: The biological functions of KNOX2 genes are somewhat elusive, but they are thought to act antagonistically to KNOX1 to promote cell differentiation (Furumizu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from cited literature.

claim: The moss genome contains three KNOX1 and two KNOX2 genes.
source: The moss genome contains three KNOX1 and two KNOX2 genes, which are all primarily expressed in sporophytes, though expression of one KNOX1 and two KNOX2 genes is additionally detected in egg cells (Horst et al., 2016; Sakakibara et al., 2013; Sakakibara et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited literature on P. patens.

claim: In Physcomitrium patens, KNOX genes are primarily expressed in sporophytes.
source: The moss genome contains three KNOX1 and two KNOX2 genes, which are all primarily expressed in sporophytes, though expression of one KNOX1 and two KNOX2 genes is additionally detected in egg cells (Horst et al., 2016; Sakakibara et al., 2013; Sakakibara et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited literature on P. patens.

claim: A triple loss-of-function mutant of all three KNOX1 genes in Physcomitrium patens was defective in cell division and differentiation in sporophytes, as well as spore formation.
source: A triple loss-of-function mutant of all three KNOX1 genes was defective in cell division and differentiation in sporophytes, as well as spore formation (Sakakibara et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited literature on P. patens.

claim: Simultaneous knockout of the two KNOX2 genes in Physcomitrium patens resulted in ectopic gametophyte formation in sporophyte bodies.
source: By contrast, simultaneous knockout of the two KNOX2 genes resulted in ectopic gametophyte formation in sporophyte bodies (Sakakibara et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited literature on P. patens.

claim: In Physcomitrium patens, KNOX1 and KNOX2 control sporophyte development via two pathways.
source: Thus, at least in one bryophyte species, KNOX1 and KNOX2 control sporophyte development via two pathways, with one ensuring proper sporophyte development (like C. reinhardtii GSM1) and the other promoting cell proliferation (like Arabidopsis KNOX1 proteins).
evidence: This is an inference based on cited literature on P. patens.

claim: Comparative transcriptome analysis identified 1583 genes with significantly decreased mRNA levels in Mprkd compared to wild-type archegonia.
source: Comparative transcriptome analysis identified 1583 and 170 genes with significantly decreased and increased mRNA levels, respectively, in Mprkd compared to wild-type archegonia, respectively (≥3-fold and false discovery rate <0.01; Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the RNA-seq analysis presented in the study.

claim: Comparative transcriptome analysis identified 170 genes with significantly increased mRNA levels in Mprkd compared to wild-type archegonia.
source: Comparative transcriptome analysis identified 1583 and 170 genes with significantly decreased and increased mRNA levels, respectively, in Mprkd compared to wild-type archegonia, respectively (≥3-fold and false discovery rate <0.01; Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the RNA-seq analysis presented in the study.

claim: MpKNOX1 is the only class I KNOX gene in Marchantia polymorpha.
source: Among the genes with reduced expression levels, MpKNOX1 (Mp5g01600), the only class I KNOX gene in M. polymorpha (Bowman et al., 2017, Frangedakis et al., 2017), showed more than 300-fold reduced expression level in Mprkd as compared to that in the wild-type (fragments per kilobase of exon per million mapped reads (FPKM) values are 19.5, 0.0629, and 0.0124 in wild-type, Mprkd-1, and Mprkd-3 archegonia, respectively; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited literature.

claim: MpKNOX1 showed more than 300-fold reduced expression level in Mprkd compared to wild-type archegonia.
source: Among the genes with reduced expression levels, MpKNOX1 (Mp5g01600), the only class I KNOX gene in M. polymorpha (Bowman et al., 2017, Frangedakis et al., 2017), showed more than 300-fold reduced expression level in Mprkd as compared to that in the wild-type (fragments per kilobase of exon per million mapped reads (FPKM) values are 19.5, 0.0629, and 0.0124 in wild-type, Mprkd-1, and Mprkd-3 archegonia, respectively; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the RNA-seq analysis.

claim: The MpKNOX1 polypeptide contains KNOX I, KNOX II, ELK, and Homeobox domains.
source: The MpKNOX1 polypeptide contains KNOX I, KNOX II, ELK, and Homeobox domains, as do KNOX proteins from green algae, mosses, ferns, and flowering plants (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a structural analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: KNOX proteins from green algae, mosses, ferns, and flowering plants contain KNOX I, KNOX II, ELK, and Homeobox domains.
source: The MpKNOX1 polypeptide contains KNOX I, KNOX II, ELK, and Homeobox domains, as do KNOX proteins from green algae, mosses, ferns, and flowering plants (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a comparative structural analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: MpKNOX1 is specifically expressed in female plants.
source: Previous RNA-sequencing data (Bowman et al., 2017) indicated that MpKNOX1 is specifically expressed in female plants (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is based on cited RNA-seq data shown in a figure.

claim: RT-PCR analysis confirmed the specific expression of MpKNOX1 in archegoniophores.
source: To obtain the detailed expression patterns of MpKNOX1, we performed RT-PCR analysis using RNA extracted from vegetative and reproductive organs of male and female gametophytes, as well as 3-week-old sporophytes, and confirmed the specific expression of MpKNOX1 in archegoniophores (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a primary finding from RT-PCR analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: No MpKNOX1 expression was detected in female or male thalli, antheridiophores, or sporophytes.
source: No expression was detected in female or male thalli (leaf-like vegetative organs), antheridiophores (male reproductive branches), or sporophytes (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a primary finding from RT-PCR analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: MpKNOX1 transcriptional reporter expression was specifically detected in egg cells.
source: Consistent with the >300-fold reduced MpKNOX1 transcript levels in egg-deficient Mprkd archegonia (Figure 1B), reporter expression was specifically detected in egg cells (Figure 2C) and not in developing archegonia before the formation of egg progenitors (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a primary finding from reporter analysis shown in Figures 2B and 2C.

claim: MpKNOX1 is an egg-specific gene in Marchantia polymorpha.
source: Together, these data indicate that MpKNOX1 is an egg-specific gene in M. polymorpha.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple lines of experimental evidence (RNA-seq, RT-PCR, reporter analysis).

claim: At the end of the 1 hr co-culture period, sperm nuclei were visible in most eggs.
source: At the end of the co-culture period, sperm nuclei were visible in most eggs (Figure 3C), indicating that fertilization had been completed during the 1 hr of co-culturing.
evidence: This is a primary observation from the in vitro fertilization experiments shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Fertilization was completed during the 1 hr of co-culturing in the in vitro fertilization method.
source: At the end of the co-culture period, sperm nuclei were visible in most eggs (Figure 3C), indicating that fertilization had been completed during the 1 hr of co-culturing.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of sperm nuclei in eggs.

claim: No cell walls were stained in mature egg cells of Marchantia polymorpha.
source: No cell walls were stained in mature egg cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), indicating that cell walls are not present in mature eggs, a prerequisite for fusion with sperm cells.
evidence: This is a primary observation from cell wall staining experiments.

claim: Cell walls are not present in mature eggs of Marchantia polymorpha, a prerequisite for fusion with sperm cells.
source: No cell walls were stained in mature egg cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), indicating that cell walls are not present in mature eggs, a prerequisite for fusion with sperm cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the absence of cell wall staining and biological knowledge.

claim: A cell wall around the zygote was detected only at 3 days after fertilization (DAF).
source: A cell wall around the zygote was detected only at 3 days after fertilization (DAF) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–D), whereas the first zygotic division occurred at 4–5 DAF (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E and F).
evidence: This is a primary observation from cell wall staining experiments.

claim: The first zygotic division in Marchantia polymorpha occurred at 4–5 DAF.
source: A cell wall around the zygote was detected only at 3 days after fertilization (DAF) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–D), whereas the first zygotic division occurred at 4–5 DAF (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E and F).
evidence: This is a primary observation from microscopy experiments.

claim: At 1–3 DAF, a male pronucleus was clearly stained with DAPI and was typically positioned halfway between the periphery and center of the fertilized egg.
source: At 1–3 DAF, a male pronucleus was clearly stained with DAPI, in contrast to the female pronucleus (not visible by DAPI staining), and was typically positioned halfway between the periphery and center of the fertilized egg (Figure 3D and E, green arrowhead).
evidence: This is a primary observation from DAPI staining experiments shown in Figures 3D and E.

claim: At 4 DAF, most zygotes completed the first division.
source: At 4 DAF, most zygotes completed the first division (Figure 3F), indicating that karyogamy takes place at 3–4 DAF.
evidence: This is a primary observation from microscopy experiments shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Karyogamy takes place at 3–4 DAF in wild-type Marchantia polymorpha.
source: At 4 DAF, most zygotes completed the first division (Figure 3F), indicating that karyogamy takes place at 3–4 DAF.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of completed first division.

claim: After 5 DAF, zygotes and the surrounding archegonial wall cells divided to form sporophytes and the calyptra.
source: After 5 DAF, zygotes and the surrounding archegonial wall cells divided to form sporophytes and the calyptra (a protective gametophyte tissue), respectively (Figure 3G–I).
evidence: This is a primary observation from microscopy experiments shown in Figures 3G-I.

claim: The in vitro fertilization protocol faithfully recapitulated fertilization programs in planta.
source: These cellular rearrangements, including karyogamy and embryogenesis, proceeded at a rate comparable to that in zygotes produced in planta (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), confirming that our in vitro fertilization protocol faithfully recapitulated fertilization programs in planta.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on comparison of in vitro and in planta observations.

claim: Three independent female mutant lines of Mpknox1 harbored nucleotide insertions or deletions resulting in premature stop codons preceding the region encoding the HD.
source: We obtained three independent female mutant lines that harbored nucleotide insertions or deletions resulting in premature stop codons preceding the region encoding the HD (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a primary finding from CRISPR/Cas9 mutagenesis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: All Mpknox1 mutants were indistinguishable from wild-type females in terms of both vegetative and reproductive morphology.
source: All mutants were indistinguishable from wild-type females in terms of both vegetative and reproductive morphology (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a primary observation from phenotypic analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Mature archegonia and egg cells of the Mpknox1 mutants were indistinguishable from those of the wild-type.
source: Mature archegonia and egg cells of the Mpknox1 mutants were also indistinguishable from those of the wild-type (Figure 4A and E), indicating that MpKNOX1 functions are dispensable for both gametophyte development and gametogenesis.
evidence: This is a primary observation from microscopy shown in Figures 4A and E.

claim: MpKNOX1 functions are dispensable for both gametophyte development and gametogenesis.
source: Mature archegonia and egg cells of the Mpknox1 mutants were also indistinguishable from those of the wild-type (Figure 4A and E), indicating that MpKNOX1 functions are dispensable for both gametophyte development and gametogenesis.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observation that mutants have normal gametophyte and gamete morphology.

claim: Each Mpknox1 egg fertilized with wild-type sperm harbored a male pronucleus at 1 DAF.
source: Similar to wild-type zygotes, each Mpknox1 egg fertilized with wild-type sperm harbored a male pronucleus at 1 DAF (Figure 4B, F and I), indicating that Mpknox1 eggs are able to fuse with wild-type sperm and support decondensation of sperm nuclei.
evidence: This is a primary observation from microscopy shown in Figures 4B, F, and I.

claim: Mpknox1 eggs are able to fuse with wild-type sperm and support decondensation of sperm nuclei.
source: Similar to wild-type zygotes, each Mpknox1 egg fertilized with wild-type sperm harbored a male pronucleus at 1 DAF (Figure 4B, F and I), indicating that Mpknox1 eggs are able to fuse with wild-type sperm and support decondensation of sperm nuclei.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observation of male pronuclei in fertilized Mpknox1 eggs.

claim: At 5 DAF, male and female pronuclei remained unfused in fertilized Mpknox1 eggs (100%, n = 34–38).
source: At 5 DAF, however, male and female pronuclei remained unfused in fertilized Mpknox1 eggs (100%, n = 34–38, Figure 4G and J), in contrast with wild-type fertilized eggs, a majority of which were undergoing sporophyte development (89%, n = 38, Figure 4C and J).
evidence: This is a primary observation from microscopy shown in Figures 4G and J.

claim: At 5 DAF, a majority of wild-type fertilized eggs were undergoing sporophyte development (89%, n = 38).
source: At 5 DAF, however, male and female pronuclei remained unfused in fertilized Mpknox1 eggs (100%, n = 34–38, Figure 4G and J), in contrast with wild-type fertilized eggs, a majority of which were undergoing sporophyte development (89%, n = 38, Figure 4C and J).
evidence: This is a primary observation from microscopy shown in Figures 4C and J.

claim: At 7 DAF, most Mpknox1 eggs contained unfused male and female pronuclei (87–94%, n = 31–56).
source: At 7 DAF, most Mpknox1 eggs contained unfused male and female pronuclei (87–94%, n = 31–56, Figure 4H and K).
evidence: This is a primary observation from microscopy shown in Figures 4H and K.

claim: The three independent Mpknox1 mutant lines exhibited indistinguishable defects in karyogamy and sporophyte development.
source: The three independent Mpknox1 mutant lines exhibited indistinguishable defects in karyogamy and sporophyte development (Figure 4I–K).
evidence: This is a primary observation from microscopy shown in Figures 4I-K.

claim: The karyogamy defects in Mpknox1 mutants were rescued in archegonia expressing MpKNOX1-GFP by the MpKNOX1 promoter.
source: Importantly, these defects were rescued in archegonia expressing MpKNOX1-GFP by the MpKNOX1 promoter (gMpKNOX1-GFP, Figure 4—figure supplement 3), confirming the notion that MpKNOX1 is required maternally to complete fertilization.
evidence: This is a primary observation from complementation experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: MpKNOX1 is required maternally to complete fertilization.
source: Importantly, these defects were rescued in archegonia expressing MpKNOX1-GFP by the MpKNOX1 promoter (gMpKNOX1-GFP, Figure 4—figure supplement 3), confirming the notion that MpKNOX1 is required maternally to complete fertilization.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the rescue of defects by maternal expression of MpKNOX1.

claim: A small fraction of Mpknox1 eggs fertilized with wild-type sperm developed into sporangia that produced functional spores.
source: A small fraction of Mpknox1 eggs fertilized with wild-type sperm developed into sporangia that produced functional spores (Figure 4—figure supplement 4), suggesting that redundant genetic pathway(s) can compensate for the loss of MpKNOX1 and/or that our Mpknox1 mutant alleles were not null, though genomic sequences preceding the HD-coding region were disrupted.
evidence: This is a primary observation from phenotypic analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: Redundant genetic pathway(s) can compensate for the loss of MpKNOX1 and/or the Mpknox1 mutant alleles were not null.
source: A small fraction of Mpknox1 eggs fertilized with wild-type sperm developed into sporangia that produced functional spores (Figure 4—figure supplement 4), suggesting that redundant genetic pathway(s) can compensate for the loss of MpKNOX1 and/or that our Mpknox1 mutant alleles were not null, though genomic sequences preceding the HD-coding region were disrupted.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observation of residual embryogenic capacity.

claim: Male Mpknox1 mutants produced functional sperm capable of producing normal embryos when used to fertilize wild-type eggs.
source: The male Mpknox1 mutants produced functional sperm capable of producing normal embryos when used to fertilize wild-type eggs (Figure 4—figure supplement 5), indicating that paternal MpKNOX1 is dispensable for gametophyte development, fertilization, and embryogenesis.
evidence: This is a primary observation from reciprocal crosses shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5.

claim: Paternal MpKNOX1 is dispensable for gametophyte development, fertilization, and embryogenesis.
source: The male Mpknox1 mutants produced functional sperm capable of producing normal embryos when used to fertilize wild-type eggs (Figure 4—figure supplement 5), indicating that paternal MpKNOX1 is dispensable for gametophyte development, fertilization, and embryogenesis.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observation that male Mpknox1 mutants produce functional sperm.

claim: Homozygous Mpknox1 zygotes exhibited karyogamy and sporangia formation defects indistinguishable from those observed in zygotes carrying maternally inherited Mpknox1 alone.
source: To further examine the lack of paternal contribution of MpKNOX1 to fertilization and sporophyte development, we crossed Mpknox1 females with Mpknox1 males. Resulting homozygous Mpknox1 zygotes exhibited the karyogamy and sporangia formation defects indistinguishable from those observed in zygotes carrying maternally inherited Mpknox1 alone (Figure 4—figure supplements 4 and 6).
evidence: This is a primary observation from crosses between Mpknox1 females and males shown in Figure 4—figure supplements 4 and 6.

claim: The egg-derived functional MpKNOX1 allele or its protein products, but not those derived from sperm, are required to activate zygote development.
source: Together, these results indicate that the egg-derived functional MpKNOX1 allele or its protein products, but not those derived from sperm, are required to activate zygote development, more specifically karyogamy, during M. polymorpha fertilization.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple genetic crosses and observations.

claim: Maternal MpKNOX1 or its protein product is required for pronuclear membrane fusion.
source: Together, these observations indicate that maternal MpKNOX1 or its protein product is dispensable for the organization and migration of pronuclei but is required for pronuclear membrane fusion.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on observations of pronuclear dynamics using MpSUN-GFP marker.

claim: Maternal MpKNOX1 or its protein product is dispensable for the organization and migration of pronuclei.
source: Together, these observations indicate that maternal MpKNOX1 or its protein product is dispensable for the organization and migration of pronuclei but is required for pronuclear membrane fusion.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on observations that pronuclei migrate normally in Mpknox1 mutants.

claim: KNOX proteins heterodimerize with BELL proteins to regulate gene transcription.
source: KNOX proteins heterodimerize with BELL proteins to regulate gene transcription (Hay and Tsiantis, 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited literature.

claim: In Chlamydomonas reinhardtii, a minus gamete-derived KNOX protein (GSM1) heterodimerizes with a plus gamete-derived BELL protein (GSP1) upon fertilization and activates the majority of early zygote-specific genes.
source: In C. reinhardtii, a minus gamete-derived KNOX protein (GSM1) heterodimerizes with a plus gamete-derived BELL protein (GSP1) upon fertilization and activates the majority of early zygote-specific genes (Joo et al., 2017; Kariyawasam et al., 2019; Lee et al., 2008; Lopez et al., 2015; Nishimura et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge from multiple cited studies.

claim: Loss of GSM1 and/or GSP1 in Chlamydomonas reinhardtii results in pronuclear fusion arrest.
source: Loss of GSM1 and/or GSP1 results in pronuclear fusion arrest, a phenotype similar to that of Mpknox1 mutants.
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited literature on C. reinhardtii.

claim: The phenotypic similarity between Marchantia polymorpha Mpknox1 and Chlamydomonas reinhardtii gsm1 mutants suggests that the role of KNOX and BELL in zygote activation is conserved.
source: The phenotypic similarity between M. polymorpha Mpknox1 and C. reinhardtii gsm1 mutants suggests that the role of KNOX and BELL in zygote activation is conserved and that its evolutionary origin can be traced back to a common ancestor of the two species.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of mutant phenotypes.

claim: The evolutionary origin of KNOX and BELL function in zygote activation can be traced back to a common ancestor of Marchantia polymorpha and Chlamydomonas reinhardtii.
source: The phenotypic similarity between M. polymorpha Mpknox1 and C. reinhardtii gsm1 mutants suggests that the role of KNOX and BELL in zygote activation is conserved and that its evolutionary origin can be traced back to a common ancestor of the two species.
evidence: This is an evolutionary inference based on the conservation of function.

claim: Two of the five BELL genes of Marchantia polymorpha, MpBELL3 and MpBELL4, are preferentially expressed in the antheridiophores of male plants.
source: In support of this hypothesis, publicly available transcriptome data (Bowman et al., 2017) indicate that two of the five BELL genes of M. polymorpha, MpBELL3 (Mp8g02970) and MpBELL4 (Mp8g07680), are preferentially expressed in the antheridiophores of male plants, whereas MpBELL1 (Mp8g18310) and MpBELL5 (Mp5g11060) are preferentially expressed in sporophytes and archegonia, respectively (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on publicly available transcriptome data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: MpBELL1 is preferentially expressed in sporophytes.
source: In support of this hypothesis, publicly available transcriptome data (Bowman et al., 2017) indicate that two of the five BELL genes of M. polymorpha, MpBELL3 (Mp8g02970) and MpBELL4 (Mp8g07680), are preferentially expressed in the antheridiophores of male plants, whereas MpBELL1 (Mp8g18310) and MpBELL5 (Mp5g11060) are preferentially expressed in sporophytes and archegonia, respectively (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on publicly available transcriptome data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: MpBELL5 is preferentially expressed in archegonia.
source: In support of this hypothesis, publicly available transcriptome data (Bowman et al., 2017) indicate that two of the five BELL genes of M. polymorpha, MpBELL3 (Mp8g02970) and MpBELL4 (Mp8g07680), are preferentially expressed in the antheridiophores of male plants, whereas MpBELL1 (Mp8g18310) and MpBELL5 (Mp5g11060) are preferentially expressed in sporophytes and archegonia, respectively (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on publicly available transcriptome data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: RT-PCR analysis confirmed that MpBELL3 and MpBELL4 are specifically expressed in antheridiophores containing antheridia.
source: RT-PCR analysis confirmed that MpBELL3 and MpBELL4 are specifically expressed in antheridiophores containing antheridia (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a primary finding from RT-PCR analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Both female and male Mpbell3/4 gametophytes grew normally.
source: Both female and male Mpbell3/4 gametophytes grew normally (Figure 4—figure supplement 2) and produced normal gametangia and gametes capable of fertilization (Figure 5—figure supplement 2, Figure 5B, D, G, J and L).
evidence: This is a primary observation from phenotypic analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Mpbell3/4 mutants produced normal gametangia and gametes capable of fertilization.
source: Both female and male Mpbell3/4 gametophytes grew normally (Figure 4—figure supplement 2) and produced normal gametangia and gametes capable of fertilization (Figure 5—figure supplement 2, Figure 5B, D, G, J and L).
evidence: This is a primary observation from phenotypic analysis shown in multiple figures.

claim: Approximately half of zygotes produced by crossing wild-type females and Mpbell3/4 males did not complete karyogamy by 5 DAF (55% and 37% for Mpbell3/4-1ge and Mpbell3/4-2ge, respectively).
source: By contrast, approximately a half of zygotes produced by crossing wild-type females and Mpbell3/4 males did not complete karyogamy by 5 DAF (55% and 37% for Mpbell3/4-1ge and Mpbell3/4-2ge, respectively; Figure 5E, F and M).
evidence: This is a primary observation from microscopy shown in Figures 5E, F, and M.

claim: Zygotes obtained from a reciprocal cross (Mpbell3/4 females with wild-type males) exhibited a low but significant degree of karyogamy arrest (30% and 22% for Mpbell3/4-1ge and Mpbell3/4-2ge, respectively).
source: Somewhat unexpectedly, zygotes obtained from a reciprocal cross (Mpbell3/4 females with wild-type males) exhibited a low but significant degree of karyogamy arrest (30% and 22% for Mpbell3/4-1ge andMpbell3/4-2ge, respectively; Figure 5H, I and M), despite the lack of detectable MpBELL3/4 expression in female gametes.
evidence: This is a primary observation from microscopy shown in Figures 5H, I, and M.

claim: A majority of 5-DAF zygotes obtained from a cross between Mpbell3/4 females and Mpbell3/4 males were arrested at karyogamy (75% and 92% for Mpbell3/4-1ge and Mpbell3/4-2ge, respectively).
source: Furthermore, a majority of 5-DAF zygotes obtained from a cross between Mpbell3/4 females and Mpbell3/4 males were arrested at karyogamy (75% and 92% for Mpbell3/4-1ge and Mpbell3/4-2ge, respectively; Figure 5K and M).
evidence: This is a primary observation from microscopy shown in Figures 5K and M.

claim: Not only paternally inherited MpBELL3 and/or MpBELL4 alleles(s) and/or their protein products, but also maternally inherited MpBELL3 and/or MpBELL4 allele(s) contribute to sporophyte development.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that not only paternally inherited MpBELL3 and/or MpBELL4 alleles(s) and/or their protein products, but also maternally inherited MpBELL3 and/or MpBELL4 allele(s) contribute to sporophyte development.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observation of karyogamy defects in various crosses.

claim: MpBELL3/4 mainly act to promote karyogamy for the progression of sporophyte development.
source: A correlation between the proportion of arrested zygotes and the degree of reduction in sporangia number in each genotype suggests that MpBELL3/4 mainly act to promote karyogamy for the progression of sporophyte development.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between karyogamy arrest and sporangia number.

claim: In mature egg cells, MpKNOX1-GFP was specifically detected in the cytosol.
source: In mature egg cells, MpKNOX1-GFP was specifically detected in the cytosol (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a primary observation from confocal microscopy shown in Figure 6A.

claim: After crossing with a wild-type male, GFP signals were detected in both male and female pronuclei at 12 hours after fertilization (83%, n = 48).
source: After crossing with a wild-type male, GFP signals were detected in both male and female pronuclei at 12 hours after fertilization (HAF) (83%, n = 48, Figure 6B and G).
evidence: This is a primary observation from confocal microscopy shown in Figures 6B and G.

claim: At 24 HAF, the GFP signals were totally excluded from the pronuclei.
source: At 24 HAF, the GFP signals were totally excluded from the pronuclei (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a primary observation from confocal microscopy shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Upon fertilization MpKNOX1 translocates from the cytosol to pronuclei.
source: These observations suggest that upon fertilization MpKNOX1 translocates from the cytosol to pronuclei.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of MpKNOX1-GFP localization changes.

claim: Approximately half of zygotes derived from a cross with Mpbell3/4 males did not exhibit nuclear-enriched GFP signals at 12 HAF (54% and 50% for Mpbell3/4-1ge and Mpbell3/4-2ge, respectively).
source: In contrast to zygotes derived from a cross with wild-type males, where GFP signals were preferentially detected in male and female pronuclei, approximately a half of zygotes derived from a cross with Mpbell3/4 males did not exhibit nuclear-enriched GFP signals at 12 HAF (54% and 50 % for Mpbell3/4-1ge and Mpbell3/4-2ge, respectively; Figure 6D and G).
evidence: This is a primary observation from confocal microscopy shown in Figures 6D and G.

claim: Paternally inherited MpBELL3 and/or MpBELL4 contribute to the pronuclear localization of MpKNOX1 after fertilization.
source: Together, these data suggest that paternally inherited MpBELL3 and/or MpBELL4 contribute to the pronuclear localization of MpKNOX1 after fertilization.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observation that nuclear enrichment of MpKNOX1-GFP is reduced in crosses with Mpbell3/4 males.

claim: MpKNOX1 is strongly expressed in developing and mature eggs.
source: Here, we demonstrated that MpKNOX1 is an egg-specific gene in M. polymorpha. MpKNOX1 is strongly expressed in developing and mature eggs, whereas no expression was detected in gametophytes, sperm, or sporophytes.
evidence: This is a summary of the expression analysis results.

claim: No MpKNOX1 expression was detected in gametophytes, sperm, or sporophytes.
source: Here, we demonstrated that MpKNOX1 is an egg-specific gene in M. polymorpha. MpKNOX1 is strongly expressed in developing and mature eggs, whereas no expression was detected in gametophytes, sperm, or sporophytes.
evidence: This is a summary of the expression analysis results.

claim: The egg-specific expression of MpKNOX1 is in sharp contrast with the expression pattern of KNOX1 genes in Physcomitrium patens.
source: The egg-specific expression of MpKNOX1 is in sharp contrast with the expression pattern of KNOX1 genes in another model bryophyte, P. patens, where all three KNOX1 genes are strongly expressed in sporophytes to regulate their development (Sakakibara et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a comparative statement based on the current findings and cited literature.

claim: A majority of egg cells produced by three independent loss-of-function Mpknox1 female mutants failed to produce embryos when fertilized with wild-type sperm.
source: Accordingly, we suspected that MpKNOX1 might function as a gamete-derived zygote activator in M. polymorpha. Indeed, a majority of egg cells produced by three independent loss-of-function Mpknox1 female mutants failed to produce embryos when fertilized with wild-type sperm.
evidence: This is a summary of the genetic analysis results.

claim: Wild-type eggs fertilized with Mpknox1 sperm produced normal embryos and spores.
source: By contrast, wild-type eggs fertilized with Mpknox1 sperm produced normal embryos and spores.
evidence: This is a summary of the reciprocal cross results.

claim: Maternal Mpknox1 has a major, if not exclusive, contribution to embryogenesis.
source: These results indicate that maternal Mpknox1 has a major, if not exclusive, contribution to embryogenesis.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the genetic crosses.

claim: MpKNOX1 produced in unfertilized eggs acts later in zygotes to initiate embryogenesis.
source: Our reporter analysis revealed that MpKNOX1 is preferentially transcribed in egg cells. By contrast, MpKNOX1-GFP accumulated in both unfertilized and fertilized eggs until 12 HAF and had mostly diminished at 24 HAF. These observations strongly argue for a mechanism in which MpKNOX1 produced in unfertilized eggs acts later in zygotes to initiate embryogenesis.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the reporter analysis and protein localization dynamics.

claim: The mode of action of MpKNOX1 is strikingly similar to that proposed for Chlamydomonas reinhardtii GSM1.
source: This mode of action of MpKNOX1 is strikingly similar to that proposed for C. reinhardtii GSM1 (Lee et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a comparative conclusion based on the current findings and cited literature.

claim: In wild-type Marchantia polymorpha karyogamy is completed only after 3–4 DAF.
source: How does egg-derived MpKNOX1 promote embryogenesis? We determined that in wild-type M. polymorpha karyogamy is completed only after 3–4 DAF.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the time-course observations.

claim: The slow progression of karyogamy is further delayed or arrested when maternal Mpknox1 is mutated.
source: This slow progression of karyogamy is further delayed or arrested when maternal Mpknox1 is mutated.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the mutant analysis.

claim: In fertilized Mpknox1 mutant eggs karyogamy was arrested at the nuclear membrane fusion step, not the nuclear migration step.
source: Observation of nuclear membrane dynamics using an MpSUN-GFP marker showed that in fertilized Mpknox1 mutant eggs karyogamy was arrested at the nuclear membrane fusion step, not the nuclear migration step.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the MpSUN-GFP marker analysis.

claim: Gamete-derived MpKNOX1 functions in pronuclei to regulate the expression of gene(s) required for nuclear membrane fusion.
source: Consistent with the predicted role of MpKNOX1 as a transcription factor, MpKNOX1-GFP localized to both male and female pronuclei by 12 HAF, far before the initiation of nuclear membrane fusion. These observations suggest that gamete-derived MpKNOX1 functions in pronuclei to regulate the expression of gene(s) required for nuclear membrane fusion, thereby activating zygote development.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the localization dynamics and mutant phenotypes.

claim: In both angiosperms and Chlamydomonas reinhardtii, the heterodimerization of KNOX and BELL is required for the nuclear translocation of these proteins.
source: In both angiosperms and C. reinhardtii, the heterodimerization of KNOX and BELL is required for the nuclear translocation of these proteins, which in turn is required for them to regulate gene transcription (Hay and Tsiantis, 2010; Lee et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited literature.

claim: Sperm-derived MpBELL3/4 are required to recruit MpKNOX1 to male and female pronuclei.
source: Consistent with this notion, our genetic and imaging analyses suggested that sperm-derived MpBELL3/4 are required to recruit MpKNOX1 to male and female pronuclei.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the genetic and imaging analyses.

claim: Maternally inherited MpBELL3 and/or MpBELL4 alleles become transcriptionally activated in zygotes.
source: A plausible explanation for this observation is that maternally inherited MpBELL3 and/or MpBELL4 alleles become transcriptionally activated in zygotes and that MpBELL3 and/or MpBELL4 expression post-fertilization acts to replenish MpBELL proteins to ensure karyogamy with high penetrance.
evidence: This is a speculation to explain the maternal contribution of MpBELL3/4.

claim: MpBELL3 and/or MpBELL4 expression post-fertilization acts to replenish MpBELL proteins to ensure karyogamy with high penetrance.
source: A plausible explanation for this observation is that maternally inherited MpBELL3 and/or MpBELL4 alleles become transcriptionally activated in zygotes and that MpBELL3 and/or MpBELL4 expression post-fertilization acts to replenish MpBELL proteins to ensure karyogamy with high penetrance.
evidence: This is a speculation to explain the maternal contribution of MpBELL3/4.

claim: Sperm-borne MpBELL3 and MpBELL4 proteins heterodimerize with egg-derived MpKNOX1 upon fertilization and activate the transcription of zygote-specific genes as well as maternal MpBELL3 and/or MpBELL4.
source: Based on these observations, we propose a two-step model of MpBELL3/4 activity (Figure 7A). According to this model, sperm-borne MpBELL3 and MpBELL4 proteins heterodimerize with egg-derived MpKNOX1 upon fertilization and activate the transcription of zygote-specific genes as well as maternal MpBELL3 and/or MpBELL4.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings shown in Figure 7A.

claim: MpBELL3 and MpBELL4 produced de novo further activate the expression of zygote-specific genes, including genes required for karyogamy.
source: MpBELL3 and MpBELL4 produced de novo further activate the expression of zygote-specific genes, including genes required for karyogamy.
evidence: This is part of the proposed two-step model.

claim: Feed-forward regulation would efficiently compensate for the presumably small amounts of MpBELL proteins inherited from the sperm cytosol.
source: Such feed-forward regulation would efficiently compensate for the presumably small amounts of MpBELL proteins inherited from the sperm cytosol.
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism of MpBELL function.

claim: A recent phenotypic analysis of newly isolated gsm1 and gsp1 alleles revealed the biparental contribution of GSM1 to karyogamy in Chlamydomonas reinhardtii.
source: Considering that a recent phenotypic analysis of newly isolated gsm1 and gsp1 alleles revealed the biparental contribution of GSM1 to karyogamy in C. reinhardtii (Kariyawasam et al., 2019), our findings further emphasize the similarity of KNOX/BELL-mediated zygote activation between M. polymorpha and C. reinhardtii.
evidence: This is established knowledge from a cited study.

claim: The findings further emphasize the similarity of KNOX/BELL-mediated zygote activation between Marchantia polymorpha and Chlamydomonas reinhardtii.
source: Considering that a recent phenotypic analysis of newly isolated gsm1 and gsp1 alleles revealed the biparental contribution of GSM1 to karyogamy in C. reinhardtii (Kariyawasam et al., 2019), our findings further emphasize the similarity of KNOX/BELL-mediated zygote activation between M. polymorpha and C. reinhardtii.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the comparison of findings with cited literature.

claim: KNOX/BELL proteins in Physcomitrium patens control sporophyte development.
source: While our study revealed the striking conservation of KNOX/BELL functions between M. polymorpha and C. reinhardtii, this finding is somewhat unexpected from a phylogenetic viewpoint because KNOX/BELL proteins in the model bryophyte P. patens control sporophyte development, as do KNOX/BELL proteins in angiosperms, as well as egg size (Sakakibara et al., 2008; Horst et al., 2016; Ortiz-Ramírez et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited literature.

claim: KNOX/BELL proteins in angiosperms control sporophyte development.
source: While our study revealed the striking conservation of KNOX/BELL functions between M. polymorpha and C. reinhardtii, this finding is somewhat unexpected from a phylogenetic viewpoint because KNOX/BELL proteins in the model bryophyte P. patens control sporophyte development, as do KNOX/BELL proteins in angiosperms, as well as egg size (Sakakibara et al., 2008; Horst et al., 2016; Ortiz-Ramírez et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited literature.

claim: TALE TFs in yeasts and fungi promote the haploid-to-diploid transition.
source: Outside the plant kingdom, TALE TFs in yeasts and fungi promote the haploid-to-diploid transition (Goutte and Johnson, 1988; Herskowitz, 1989; Kues et al., 1992, Spit et al., 1998).
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited literature.

claim: The shared zygote-activating functions of KNOX/BELL in Marchantia polymorpha and Chlamydomonas reinhardtii reflect an ancestral state.
source: Thus, perhaps the shared zygote-activating functions of KNOX/BELL in M. polymorpha and C. reinhardtii reflect an ancestral state (Bowman et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an evolutionary inference based on the conservation of function and cited literature.

claim: The functional transition of KNOX/BELLs from zygote activation to sporophyte morphogenesis occurred at least twice during land plant evolution.
source: Considering the generally accepted view of bryophyte monophyly (de Sousa et al., 2019; Puttick et al., 2018), our findings suggest that the functional transition of KNOX/BELLs from zygote activation to sporophyte morphogenesis occurred at least twice during land plant evolution, including once in the bryophyte lineage and once in the tracheophyte lineage (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is an evolutionary inference based on the phylogenetic distribution of functions shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The functional transition of KNOX/BELLs occurred once in the bryophyte lineage and once in the tracheophyte lineage.
source: Considering the generally accepted view of bryophyte monophyly (de Sousa et al., 2019; Puttick et al., 2018), our findings suggest that the functional transition of KNOX/BELLs from zygote activation to sporophyte morphogenesis occurred at least twice during land plant evolution, including once in the bryophyte lineage and once in the tracheophyte lineage (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is an evolutionary inference based on the phylogenetic distribution of functions shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The zygote-activating function of KNOX/BELL is conserved between Chlamydomonas reinhardtii and Marchantia polymorpha.
source: Our study revealed that the zygote-activating function of KNOX/BELL is conserved between C. reinhardtii and M. polymorpha, which belong to Chlorophyta and Streptophyta, respectively.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding.

claim: Chlorophyta and Streptophyta were separated more than 700 million years ago.
source: These two major green plant lineages were separated more than 700 million years ago (Becker, 2013; Figure 7B).
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited literature shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The sex-specific expression patterns of KNOX and BELL in Chlamydomonas reinhardtii are opposite to those in Marchantia polymorpha.
source: Interestingly, however, the sex-specific expression patterns of KNOX and BELL in C. reinhardtii are opposite to those in M. polymorpha.
evidence: This is a comparative conclusion based on the expression analyses.

claim: In Chlamydomonas reinhardtii, KNOX (GSM1) is expressed in isogamous minus gametes.
source: In C. reinhardtii, KNOX (GSM1) and BELL (GSP1) are expressed in isogamous minus and plus gametes (Lee et al., 2008), which directly evolved into male and female gametes, respectively, in oogamous (with small motile gametes and large immotile gametes) Volvox carteri, primarily by modifying genes acting downstream of the conserved sex-determinant protein MID (Ferris and Goodenough, 1997; Geng et al., 2014; Geng et al., 2018; Nozaki et al., 2006; Figure 7B).
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited literature shown in Figure 7B.

claim: In Chlamydomonas reinhardtii, BELL (GSP1) is expressed in isogamous plus gametes.
source: In C. reinhardtii, KNOX (GSM1) and BELL (GSP1) are expressed in isogamous minus and plus gametes (Lee et al., 2008), which directly evolved into male and female gametes, respectively, in oogamous (with small motile gametes and large immotile gametes) Volvox carteri, primarily by modifying genes acting downstream of the conserved sex-determinant protein MID (Ferris and Goodenough, 1997; Geng et al., 2014; Geng et al., 2018; Nozaki et al., 2006; Figure 7B).
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited literature shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Minus and plus gametes in Chlamydomonas reinhardtii directly evolved into male and female gametes, respectively, in oogamous Volvox carteri.
source: In C. reinhardtii, KNOX (GSM1) and BELL (GSP1) are expressed in isogamous minus and plus gametes (Lee et al., 2008), which directly evolved into male and female gametes, respectively, in oogamous (with small motile gametes and large immotile gametes) Volvox carteri, primarily by modifying genes acting downstream of the conserved sex-determinant protein MID (Ferris and Goodenough, 1997; Geng et al., 2014; Geng et al., 2018; Nozaki et al., 2006; Figure 7B).
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited literature shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The expression specificity of KNOX/BELL is conserved along the volvocine lineage.
source: Results from other research groups indicate that the expression specificity of KNOX/BELL is conserved along the volvocine lineage (with minus and male gametes expressing GSM1, and plus and female gametes expressing GSP1; personal communication with Takashi Hamaji [Kyoto University, Japan] and James Umen [Donald Danforth Plant Science Center, MO]).
evidence: This is based on personal communications with other researchers.

claim: In at least one Chlorophyta lineage, KNOX and BELL are expressed in male and female gametes, respectively, a situation opposite to that in Marchantia polymorpha.
source: Thus, at least in one Chlorophyta lineage, KNOX and BELL are expressed in male and female gametes, respectively, a situation opposite to that in M. polymorpha (KNOX for females and BELL for males; Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a comparative conclusion based on the expression patterns shown in Figure 7B.

claim: In land plants, oogamy likely evolved once.
source: In land plants, oogamy likely evolved once as key regulators of gametophytic sexual differentiation, such as FGMYBs for females and DUO POLLEN 1 (DUO1) for males, are shared between M. polymorpha and Arabidopsis (see Hisanaga et al., 2019b for a review; Figure 7B).
evidence: This is an evolutionary inference based on the conservation of key regulators shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Key regulators of gametophytic sexual differentiation, such as FGMYBs for females and DUO1 for males, are shared between Marchantia polymorpha and Arabidopsis.
source: In land plants, oogamy likely evolved once as key regulators of gametophytic sexual differentiation, such as FGMYBs for females and DUO POLLEN 1 (DUO1) for males, are shared between M. polymorpha and Arabidopsis (see Hisanaga et al., 2019b for a review; Figure 7B).
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited literature shown in Figure 7B.

claim: In ancestral green plants, KNOX/BELL expression specificity did not affect gamete morphology or function.
source: Theoretical analyses predicted that anisogamy evolved through disruptive selection, where an increased volume of one type of gamete favors zygote fitness, allowing the other gamete type to increase in number at the expense of volume (Parker et al., 1972). Thus, in ancestral green plants, KNOX/BELL expression specificity did not affect gamete morphology or function.
evidence: This is an inference based on theoretical analyses from cited literature.

claim: Neither MpKNOX1 nor MpBELL3/4 contribute to gamete development or function in extant Marchantia polymorpha.
source: This notion is consistent with our observation that neither MpKNOX1 nor MpBELL3/4 contribute to gamete development or function in extant M. polymorpha.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observation that mutants have normal gametes.

claim: The study revealed a critical role of KNOX and BELL in zygote activation in the model bryophyte Marchantia polymorpha.
source: In summary, our study revealed a critical role of KNOX and BELL in zygote activation in the model bryophyte M. polymorpha.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding.

claim: The role of KNOX and BELL in zygote activation is in stark contrast with the well-recognized role of KNOX/BELL in sporophytic meristem maintenance in angiosperms and Physcomitrium patens.
source: This is in stark contrast with a well-recognized role of KNOX/BELL in sporophytic meristem maintenance in angiosperms and another model bryophyte P. patens.
evidence: This is a comparative statement based on the current findings and established knowledge.

claim: Striking conservation of KNOX/BELL functions in the promotion of karyogamy across phylogenetically distant Marchantia polymorpha and Chlamydomonas reinhardtii suggests that functions of KNOX/BELL heterodimers shifted from zygote activation to sporophyte development as land plants evolved.
source: Rather, striking conservation of KNOX/BELL functions in the promotion of karyogamy across phylogenetically distant M. polymorpha and C. reinhardtii suggests that functions of KNOX/BELL heterodimers shifted from zygote activation to sporophyte development as land plants evolved.
evidence: This is an evolutionary inference based on the conservation of function.

claim: This view is consistent with a proposed evolutionary scenario of HD proteins in broader eukaryotic taxa, including fungi and metazoans.
source: This view is consistent with a proposed evolutionary scenario of HD proteins in broader eukaryotic taxa, including fungi and metazoans (Bowman et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a statement connecting the findings to a broader evolutionary framework from cited literature.
